extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature; literary critics and scholars interested in Goethe, the novel, and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for assessing Goethe's Wilhelm Meister and related writings: their moral, aesthetic, and social significance, treatment of vocation, art, science, religion, and the relations of the sexes, within the context of Goethe's life and corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel as large-scale treatment of opinions or views of life
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the first important instance of a novel which deals principally and on a large scale with opinions or views of life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The work should be judged as a systematic presentation of views about life rather than merely an entertaining tale; compare its aims and scope with other novel forms (e.g., Waverley Novels) and note its role as a model for the modern novel that attempts to teach or present a practical/artistic side.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of instructiveness versus amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is throughout most seriously instructive; it is seldom very amusing; and we may add that the moral of the story is not brought out with very convincing distinctness."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the novel successfully instructs without being merely dull; assess clarity and force of the moral lesson and whether didacticism undermines engagement. Antipattern: treating instructiveness as equivalent to entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual coherence with author’s other works and life
rubrics_metrics.description: "It can never be fully appreciated when it is considered by itself, but must be judged in the closest connection with his other works and with his life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess themes and moral positions in relation to Goethe's broader corpus and biography. Consider how personal experience and other writings illuminate or temper the novel's claims; avoid isolated readings that ignore authorial development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of vocations/occupation as central moral problem
rubrics_metrics.description: "Goethe begins with the fact that each man has an occupation... the principal problem to secure that this occupation should be not only worthy, but suited to the capacity of the individual and pursued in a serious spirit... the greatest of all duties, that of choosing one’s occupation rightly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge how the novel frames 'vocation' as ethical priority: does it convincingly argue that choosing/fulfilling a suitable occupation is central to moral life and inward harmony? Examples: analysis of Wilhelm’s mistake and stages toward clearness. Score higher when occupation is shown as philosophically and poetically significant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraying work/business as philosophically and poetically worthy
rubrics_metrics.description: "The distinction of 'Wilhelm Meister' that it is actually a novel about business... an attempt to show that the occupation to which a man gives his life is a matter not only for serious thought, but that it is a matter also for philosophy and poetry."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate success in making quotidian occupations interesting and meaningful; assess whether the text 'creates the taste' necessary for appreciating business-as-life. Anti-pattern: treating work merely as background routine, confining moral interest to leisure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realism that rescues work from dulness
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is the distinction of 'Wilhelm Meister'... his peculiar realism at once prompts and enables him to introduce a reform here. He denies that business is uninteresting..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for concrete realist detail that renders work-life vivid and worthy of contemplation. Reward passages that shift readers' tastes to appreciate business, and penalize flattened or romanticized depictions that fail to engage the realities of occupation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between positive and negative parts of moral scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: "We may distinguish between the positive and the negative part of this moral scheme... All that 'Wilhelm Meister' contains on the subject of vocations seems valuable..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate and evaluate affirmative teachings (e.g., vocation theory) from negative omissions or one-sidedness. Assess whether positive insights compensate for or mitigate problematic aspects; note where innovator's reaction to orthodox morality leads to opposite excesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding one-sided innovation in moral argument
rubrics_metrics.description: "Such attempts are always likely to be one-sided... the innovator is apt to be hurried into the opposite extreme, and to overlook in his turn what the orthodox morality has taught rightly."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique the novel for tendencies to overcorrect orthodox views; check for blind spots where reactionary emphasis neglects valid moral traditions. Prefer balanced treatment that acknowledges both oversight and valid teachings of orthodoxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art and Science as twin modes of religious contemplation
rubrics_metrics.description: "Art and Science taken together, the living, loving, worshipping contemplation of Nature, out of which comes the knowledge of Nature, are to Goethe religion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess portrayal of Art and Science as integrated, reverent practices akin to religion; evaluate passages where contemplation yields moral or spiritual insight. Penalize narrow, purely analytical depictions of science that separate feeling and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of 'dry' analytical science in favor of integrated wonder
rubrics_metrics.description: "Science, according to 'Faust,' must not be dry analysis pursued at a desk... man must converse with Nature 'as one spirit with another'... How we should not study is conveyed... by the picture of Wagner... the ordinary man of science... 'the dry creeper.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate temper and method of inquiry valorized by the work: does it favor loving, holistic inquiry over atomistic investigation? Use character foils (e.g., Wagner) as evidence of the author's stance; penalize didactic praise of dispassionate, narrowly technical methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced depiction of feminine vocations and character-types
rubrics_metrics.description: "In the later books... we have a view of feminine vocations. The 'Beautiful Soul' represents the pietistic view... Therese appears... economic or utilitarian view; finally, Natalie hits the golden mean..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether female characters are presented as distinct vocational types with moral and psychological credibility. Reward nuanced contrasts (pietistic, utilitarian, balanced) and critique reductive or stereotyped portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of Christianity and relation to religion
rubrics_metrics.description: "He was... half aware that there was all the difference... between the Christianity of his time and original Christianity... he keeps open for himself the alternative of appearing as a reformer rather than an assailant of it... in the Autobiography he appears, on the whole, as a Christian."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how the novel (and the author) negotiates Christianity: as opponent, reformer, or reconciler. Consider whether distinctions between clericalism and true Christianity are recognized and whether the work offers a conciliatory or polemical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness regarding relations of the sexes
rubrics_metrics.description: "What surprises the English reader... is also the extraordinary levity with which it treats the relations of men and women... More correctly speaking, it is immoral throughout on one point; immoral... in Goethe’s peculiar... good-natured manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge the work's treatment of sexual and romantic ethics: does it treat relations with warranted gravity or with libertine levity? Cite examples (Elective Affinities, Roman Elegies, character behavior) and note cultural/contextual influences, but penalize avoidant or cavalier moral treatment when social consequences are ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical/antique influence on sexual morals (Hetaeræ model)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He found that in the ancient world friendship is more and love less... he accustomed his imagination to the lower kind of love... the Hetaeræ of old Greek cities."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how imitation of classical models shapes representations of love and women: is recourse to antiquity used to justify reduced seriousness or to illuminate differences? Evaluate appropriateness and consequences of adopting ancient erotic ideals in a modern moral context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of love as transient and authorial insensitivity to consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: "One love-passage succeeds another, each is charmingly described, but each comes speedily to an end... he never looks back... a curious insensibility... Faust never once mentions Gretchen again..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine narrative consequences for characters abandoned or harmed by fleeting passions; assess whether the text affords proper moral reckoning, remorse, or continuity of emotional consequence. Penalize structural forgetfulness (sudden omission of past affections) as moral or artistic failing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of political/social reform engagement versus cultural reform
rubrics_metrics.description: "He was a reformer on the great scale in literature, art, education, that is, in culture, but he was not a reformer of institutions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating social significance, distinguish cultural/intellectual reform from advocacy for institutional change; assess whether the work's moral prescriptions presuppose or ignore problematic social institutions, and whether that limits the work's practical moral influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial tone: sincerity versus cold irony
rubrics_metrics.description: "The tone of cold irony is not by any means congenial to him... His view of life and literature is, in general, not ironical and not enervating, but sincere, manly, and hopeful."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the dominant tone—whether ironic detachment or heartfelt sincerity—and the effect on moral teaching and reader persuasion. Reward consistent, engaged tone that supports ethical teaching; critique excessive irony that produces 'cold unwholesome exhalation' of moral decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall moral status: partial indifferentism vs substantial moral teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not morality itself that he regards with indifference, but one important section of morality... he remains a moralist; and in his positive teaching he is one of the greatest moral teachers the world has ever seen."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh isolated moral lapses (e.g., sexual levity) against the author's broader moral contributions: evaluate the work's net moral effect, recognizing valuable positive teaching alongside significant reservations. Consider historical shifts that mitigate particular failings (e.g., elevation of women in nineteenth century).
